items.title: 31.5 Fractional Distillation and Refining of Petroleum

source_refs.note: Topic 31.5 with Figure 31.6 (redrawn), its labels as a table, and Quick Check 31.3 as printed (PDF 225-226); kerosene C₁₀H₁₄ and lubricating oils C₁₅-C₂₀ are marked with a Book correction.

blocks.text: Crude oil is a complicated mixture of hydrocarbons and it needs separation into simpler and useful hydrocarbons. This separation process is done physically by a method known as fractional distillation which depends on the difference in boiling points of different hydrocarbons. During this process, the crude oil is heated inside a furnace until it is vaporized. The vapor is then passed to a fractionating column, a tall tower through which the temperature drops slowly going up.

Since the vapor travels upwards, various hydrocarbon constituents condense at various points in the column based on their boiling points. Hydrocarbons that are heavier have higher boiling point are condensed closer to the bottom, whereas lighter hydrocarbons with low boiling point rises further. The process enables the extraction of useful fractions of crude oil which are given below with their uses in Figure 31.6.

blocks.alt: A fractionating column, hottest at the bottom, fed with hot vaporized crude oil from a furnace, with a temperature bar from <20 C at the top to >370 C at the bottom and six outlets to labelled fractions.
blocks.caption: Figure 31.6: Fractional distillation of crude oil into useful hydrocarbons (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 31.6).
blocks.long_description: A tall fractionating column, hottest (red) at the bottom and coolest (pale yellow) at the top, with trays and upward blue arrows. Left: a temperature bar from less than 20 C at the top to more than 370 C at the bottom; crude oil input passes through a furnace and enters the column as hot vaporized crude oil. Six outlets lead to boxes: top of the column, Gases (e.g., LPG) <25 C, cooking and heating; Gasoline (petrol) C8H18, <40 C - 200 C, fuel for cars and bikes; Kerosene C10H22, 150-275 C, jet fuel, lamps; Diesel C14-C19, 250-350 C, trucks, buses, generators; Lubricating oils C15-C20, 300-370 C, engine oil, grease; Residue (bitumen) C20+, >370 C, road surfacing, roofing.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Figure 31.6 prints kerosene as C₁₀H₁₄, which is not an alkane formula (CₙH₂ₙ₊₂); a typical kerosene alkane is C₁₀H₂₂ (decane), and kerosene is roughly C₁₀ to C₁₆. It prints lubricating oils as C₁₅-C₂₀, almost the diesel range; lubricating oils are heavier than diesel, about C₂₀ to C₅₀. The figure above is drawn with C₁₀H₂₂ and C₂₀-C₅₀.
Fractional distillation is an important process as it provides petrochemicals having applications in industries, domestic, and transportation purposes.
